questions.q: What does "consumer awareness" mean in simple terms?
questions.a: It means knowing your rights as a buyer and how to protect yourself from unfair practices like being overcharged or sold bad products. A wrong answer here suggests the student thinks it is just about "finding cheap prices" rather than protecting their legal rights as a consumer.

questions.q: Why is the "Right to be informed" important when buying a new school bag or a food item?
questions.a: It is important because it ensures you know the price, ingredients, or durability of the product before you hand over your money. If a student says "it doesn't matter," they fail to understand that information prevents them from being cheated by hidden costs or poor quality.

questions.q: You go to a shop and the seller refuses to show the expiry date on a bottle of juice. Which right are they violating, and what should you do?
questions.a: They are violating your "Right to be informed." You should firmly ask to see the label and, if they refuse, choose not to buy from that shop to protect your health and money. A wrong answer suggests the student thinks they must just accept the seller's word, missing the point of active consumer protection.

questions.q: If a company sells a toy that breaks easily and injures a child, which consumer right has been ignored?
questions.a: The "Right to safety." This reveals that the product did not meet the standard of being safe for its intended use; a wrong answer implies the student believes "buyer beware" (it's the buyer's fault for buying it), which ignores the responsibility of the seller.

questions.q: Is it better to buy products with labels or products sold without any packaging/info in a local market? Why?
questions.a: It is better to buy products with labels because they provide information required by your "Right to be informed," making it easier to hold the seller accountable. A wrong answer suggests the student prioritizes convenience over the security of knowing what they are purchasing.

questions.q: Imagine you are an inspector. What three things would you tell a new shopkeeper to always do to be a "consumer-friendly" seller?
questions.a: The shopkeeper should: 1) Display prices clearly, 2) Never sell expired goods, and 3) Be honest about product quality. A poor answer would focus only on "being nice" rather than providing the transparent information and safety a consumer deserves.

questions.q: Fill in the blank: Consumer awareness is the process of ______ your rights as a buyer and learning how to protect yourself from unfair market practices like overcharging, selling defective goods, or adulteration.
Fill in the blank: Have you ever bought a packet of chips only to find it was already ______, or felt you were charged more than the price printed on the label?
What is Consumer awareness? State the definition given in this lesson.
questions.a: Consumer awareness is the process of understanding your rights as a buyer and learning how to protect yourself from unfair market practices like overcharging, selling defective goods, or adulteration.

questions.q: What common mix-up does this lesson flag about Consumer awareness?
questions.a: Students often confuse "consumer rights" with "being rude to shopkeepers." They think being an "aware" consumer means arguing or fighting with a seller.

questions.q: What must you be able to do to master this topic?
questions.a: The student must be able to identify at least two consumer rights and explain how a consumer can use them to avoid being cheated by a seller in a local market scenario.
